content:
Structured data is a block of machine-readable code, usually JSON-LD, that tells search engines plainly who you are, where you are and what a page is about. For a web development company in Pune, or any local business with a website, the useful set is small: Organization markup on the home page, LocalBusiness markup that matches your real address and phone number, Article markup on blog posts, and BreadcrumbList on inner pages. It does not guarantee a rating, a rich result or a higher rank. What it does is remove guesswork, and that is worth an afternoon's work if you do it honestly and keep it in step with what visitors can actually see.

This guide is for owners of Pune businesses and the marketers or developers who maintain their websites. It explains which schema types are worth adding, which properties Google lists as required or recommended, how to write the code, where to put it, and how to test it. It also covers a change that catches people out: Google has stopped showing FAQ rich results, so adding FAQ markup in the hope of getting expandable questions in search is no longer a reason to do it. We will say what is still worth doing and what is not, and we will be clear about what we could not verify.

## What Structured Data Is, and What It Is Not

A search engine reads your page much as a visitor does, but it has to infer meaning from layout and words. Structured data states the meaning outright. A page might show "Landmark Plaza, Satara Road, Pune" in a footer, and a person understands it is an office address. Markup says the same thing in a form software cannot misread: this is a postal address, this is a telephone number, and both belong to this organisation.

The vocabulary comes from schema.org, a shared dictionary of types and properties. Google reads that vocabulary and documents which types it uses to power particular search features. The three common ways of writing it are JSON-LD, Microdata and RDFa. Google's general guidelines list JSON-LD as the recommended format, and it is the easiest to maintain because it sits in one script block rather than being woven through your HTML.

Three limits are worth stating plainly before you start:

- **Markup does not create rankings.** Google says valid markup does not guarantee a rich result will appear; the algorithm decides what to show. Treat it as clarity, not a lever.
- **Markup must describe visible content.** Google's guidelines say structured data must describe content users can see on the page. If your markup claims something the page does not show, you risk a manual action that removes rich result eligibility.
- **Markup does not fix a weak page.** If the page is thin, slow or confusing, tidy code will not help. The fundamentals come first, which is why we treat this as a finishing layer after the work described in our guide to [headings, alt text and semantic HTML](/blog/web-development-company-pune-image-alt-text-headings-semantic-html-seo-2026).

## Which Schema Types Does a Pune Business Website Actually Need?

It is tempting to paste every type a plugin offers. Resist that. Each type should map to something real on a real page. A sensible baseline for a service business looks like this:

| Page | Schema type | Why it earns its place |
|---|---|---|
| Home page | Organization (or the more specific LocalBusiness) | States name, logo, address, phone and official profiles |
| Contact or location page | LocalBusiness with address and opening hours | Matches your Google Business Profile details |
| Blog posts | Article or BlogPosting | Names the headline, author, publish and modified dates |
| Inner pages | BreadcrumbList | Shows the page's position in your site structure |
| Online store product pages | Product with Offer | Covered in our separate product-page guide |

Things most small businesses should skip: review markup for your own business (Google's LocalBusiness documentation says aggregate rating and review properties are for sites that capture reviews about other local businesses, not self-serving ones), markup for content that is not on the page, and any type added only because a competitor appears to have it.

## Organization Markup: The Home Page Foundation

Google's Organization documentation says there are no required properties, and recommends adding every property that applies. The properties it highlights include name, alternate name, address, telephone, URL and logo, and it also lists sameAs, email and contactPoint among others. Google recommends putting this markup on your home page or on a single page that describes your organisation, such as an About page. You do not need it on every page.

Here is a worked example for a made-up business, "Example Interiors Pune". Replace every value with your own details.

```
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "name": "Example Interiors Pune",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/",
  "logo": "https://www.example.com/images/logo.png",
  "telephone": "+91-00000-00000",
  "email": "hello@example.com",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "Shop 4, Example Plaza, Example Road",
    "addressLocality": "Pune",
    "addressRegion": "Maharashtra",
    "postalCode": "411000",
    "addressCountry": "IN"
  },
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.facebook.com/exampleinteriors",
    "https://www.instagram.com/exampleinteriors"
  ]
}
</script>
```

A few practical notes on that block:

- The logo should be a crawlable image file at a stable address. A logo that only exists as a background in a stylesheet is harder for a search engine to use.
- The sameAs list should contain only official profiles you control. Do not list directories you merely appear on.
- The telephone should be written in international format. Use the same number everywhere, which matters more than it sounds, as our article on [local citations and directory listings](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-local-citations-justdial-sulekha-directory-listings-2026) explains.

## LocalBusiness Markup: Matching What You Tell Google Elsewhere

LocalBusiness is a more specific type than Organization and is a better fit when you serve customers at a physical place. Google's documentation lists address and name as required, and lists several recommended properties: geo coordinates, opening hours, price range, telephone and URL, among others.

You can use a more specific subtype if one exists that truly fits, such as a dental clinic, a restaurant or a store. Google's guidance is to use the most specific applicable type. If you are a service business with no matching subtype, LocalBusiness itself is fine.

Opening hours deserve care. Mark them up only if they are accurate and published on the page. A mismatch between your markup, your page and your Google Business Profile is the sort of inconsistency that confuses customers and search engines alike. A short example:

```
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "name": "Example Interiors Pune",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/contact/",
  "telephone": "+91-00000-00000",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "Shop 4, Example Plaza, Example Road",
    "addressLocality": "Pune",
    "addressRegion": "Maharashtra",
    "postalCode": "411000",
    "addressCountry": "IN"
  },
  "geo": {
    "@type": "GeoCoordinates",
    "latitude": 18.0000,
    "longitude": 73.0000
  },
  "openingHoursSpecification": [{
    "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
    "dayOfWeek": ["Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Friday","Saturday"],
    "opens": "10:00",
    "closes": "19:00"
  }]
}
```

The coordinates above are placeholders. Take yours from your actual map pin, and do not guess.

### Should a service-area business add an address?

If customers do not visit you, and you travel to them, think about whether publishing a street address on the page helps anyone. Markup must reflect what is shown on the page. If your address is private, do not publish it in markup either. You can describe the area you serve in visible text and consider the areaServed property, but only if your page genuinely says where you work. For the Google Business Profile side of this decision, see our guide to [local SEO and the Google map pack in Pune](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026).

## Article Markup for Blog Posts

Article markup tells a search engine the headline, author, and dates of a post. Google does not list a strict required set for generic Article markup in the way it does for some rich result types, but it recommends including properties such as the author, headline, image and the dates the page was published and modified. A reasonable minimal block looks like this:

```
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BlogPosting",
  "headline": "How to Plan a Website Redesign",
  "datePublished": "2026-11-17",
  "dateModified": "2026-11-17",
  "author": {
    "@type": "Organization",
    "name": "Example Interiors Pune"
  },
  "image": "https://www.example.com/images/redesign-plan.jpg",
  "mainEntityOfPage": "https://www.example.com/blog/redesign-plan/"
}
```

Two honesty points apply here. First, only change dateModified when you have genuinely changed the content in a meaningful way; bumping it to look fresh is the kind of trick that erodes trust. Second, the author should be a real person or organisation named visibly on the page. A byline in the markup that does not appear to readers breaks the visible-content rule.

## BreadcrumbList for Inner Pages

Breadcrumb markup describes where a page sits in your hierarchy: Home, then Services, then Website Design. It is low risk and low effort, and it should mirror a breadcrumb trail shown on the page. If your pages do not display breadcrumbs, either add a visible trail or skip the markup. Marking up navigation that does not exist is exactly what the guidelines warn against.

## FAQ Markup: What Changed and What To Do Now

Many Pune business sites added FAQ markup over the past few years in the hope of getting expandable question boxes under their search listing. Google's documentation page for FAQ structured data now states that the FAQ rich result feature is no longer shown in Google Search results, with the end date given in the page's change notes as 7 May 2026. We read this from Google's own documentation at the time of writing; check the page again before you decide, because documentation changes.

What follows from this:

- **Do not add FAQ markup expecting a visual search feature.** There is nothing to win there now.
- **Do keep a visible FAQ section if it helps visitors.** A short list of honest questions answers real customer worries, reduces repeat phone calls, and gives the page useful text. That value does not depend on markup.
- **Existing FAQ markup is not a violation by itself,** provided it mirrors visible questions and answers. There is no need to hurry to delete it, but do not spend new budget adding more.

A good rule: write FAQs for people first. If the markup is easy to generate from the visible text, fine. If it is a project in itself, spend the time elsewhere.

## Where To Put the Code and How To Add It

The practical steps differ by platform.

### WordPress

An SEO plugin will usually generate Organization and Article markup for you, and often BreadcrumbList too. The risk is duplicates: a theme and a plugin both outputting an Organization block, with different phone numbers. Check the page source and look for more than one block of the same type. Fix the source of the problem rather than layering another plugin on top. If you need custom LocalBusiness markup, a small snippet in the theme or a header-scripts field is enough; avoid pasting code into several places.

### Custom-built sites

If your site is built in a framework, add the JSON-LD as part of the page template, generated from the same data that renders the visible content. This is the best approach because the markup and the page cannot drift apart: the address in the footer and the address in the JSON-LD come from one record. A static copy pasted into one template will go stale the next time the phone number changes.

### Shopify and WooCommerce

Both platforms output Product markup by default in many themes. You will often need to check it rather than write it. We cover that in our separate article on [product pages and product markup for online stores](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-page-structure-product-schema-merchant-listings-2026).

## Testing Your Markup

Test in two stages: syntax, then truth.

1. **Syntax.** Google offers a Rich Results Test for features that it supports, and the Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org for general schema.org checking. Paste a URL or the code and fix errors. A missing comma in JSON-LD can invalidate the whole block.
2. **Truth.** Read the markup next to the visible page. Is every value in the markup shown to the visitor? Does the phone number match the footer, the contact page and your Google Business Profile? Is the opening time right on a Sunday?
3. **Indexing.** Use the URL Inspection tool in Search Console to see whether Google has crawled the page, and check that the page is not blocked. Google's guidelines say not to block pages carrying structured data from Googlebot with robots.txt or noindex. If you are unsure how those controls differ, our guide to [robots.txt and noindex](/blog/web-development-company-pune-robots-txt-noindex-staging-site-google-index-2026) explains it.
4. **Monitoring.** Search Console reports on structured data types it detects. Review the report after a redesign, a theme change or a plugin update, because those are the moments markup breaks.

## Common Mistakes We See

- **Markup that contradicts the page.** The classic case is a phone number in the code from two years ago.
- **Self-serving review markup.** Marking up your own reviews as a LocalBusiness rating, against Google's documented guidance for that type.
- **Duplicate blocks.** A plugin, a theme and a manual snippet all describing the same organisation.
- **Invisible content.** Marking up an FAQ, a product or an author that the page never shows.
- **Expecting instant results.** Google says valid markup does not guarantee a feature will display, and crawling takes time.
- **Never revisiting.** Markup should be part of a website maintenance routine, in the same way you would update opening hours for Diwali.

## A Realistic Time Estimate

For a small business site of ten to twenty pages, the work is modest. These are our rough working estimates, not benchmarks from a study:

- Organization block on the home page: well under an hour including testing.
- LocalBusiness on the contact page: about an hour, mostly spent confirming the details.
- Article markup via an SEO plugin or template: an hour or two the first time, then automatic.
- A full audit of what is already on the site, to find duplicates and stale values: half a day.

If a quotation lists "schema markup" as a large separate cost, ask what exactly is being built and whether it is already included in the SEO or build scope. Our [website maintenance guide](/blog/website-maintenance-support-pune-guide-2026) explains how to separate one-off work from ongoing care.

## A Short Checklist You Can Use Today

1. List the pages that need markup and the type each one needs.
2. Gather your real business details in one document: name, address, phone, hours, logo, profiles.
3. Check what your CMS or plugin already outputs by viewing the page source.
4. Remove duplicates before adding anything.
5. Add or correct Organization on the home page and LocalBusiness on the contact page.
6. Confirm that Article markup names a real, visible author and honest dates.
7. Test syntax, then compare to visible content.
8. Recheck after any redesign or plugin update.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does schema markup improve Google rankings?
Google does not describe structured data as a ranking factor, and it says valid markup does not guarantee a rich result. Use it for clarity and eligibility for features, not as a ranking shortcut.

### Should I use JSON-LD, Microdata or RDFa?
Google lists JSON-LD as the recommended format. It sits in a single script block, so it is easier to maintain than markup woven through your page HTML.

### Is FAQ schema still worth adding in 2026?
Google's documentation says the FAQ rich result is no longer shown in search results. A visible FAQ section can still help visitors, but do not add FAQ markup expecting a search feature.

### What is the difference between Organization and LocalBusiness markup?
Organization describes a company in general and is recommended on the home page or an About page. LocalBusiness is a more specific type for a business with a physical location, and Google lists name and address as required for it.

### Can I add review stars to my own business using schema?
Google's LocalBusiness documentation says aggregate rating and review properties are for sites that capture reviews about other local businesses, so do not use them to mark up reviews of your own business.
